title: Halmos two-projection decomposition
subtitle: G2 lecture 045000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: The full geometry of two projections
slides.lead: Principal planes describe tilted pairs, but arbitrary subspaces also have common and unmatched directions.
body: Let P and Q project orthogonally onto closed subspaces U and V. Halmos’s decomposition first extracts four elementary intersections on which P and Q are each either I or 0.
Their orthogonal complement is the generic part where neither projection has a trivial common or defect direction. Both projections preserve that remainder.
slides.takeaway: Classifying two projections begins by separating four endpoint spaces from the generic part.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 045000 · The full geometry of two projections

slides.title: The four elementary spaces
slides.lead: Label a direction by whether it belongs to U and whether it belongs to V.
body: H₁₁=U∩V is common to both. H₁₀=U∩V⊥ belongs only to U. H₀₁=U⊥∩V belongs only to V. H₀₀=U⊥∩V⊥ belongs to neither.
On these spaces the projector pair (P,Q) acts respectively as (1,1), (1,0), (0,1), and (0,0). This completely determines both projections on their elementary sum.
slides.mathtex: H_{11}=U\cap V,\quad H_{10}=U\cap V^\perp,\quad H_{01}=U^\perp\cap V,\quad H_{00}=U^\perp\cap V^\perp
slides.takeaway: Each elementary space records a distinct membership pattern.

slides.title: Why those spaces are orthogonal
slides.lead: Every two different membership patterns disagree in at least one orthogonality condition.
body: For example, H₁₁ and H₁₀ both lie in U, but one lies in V and the other in V⊥. Therefore they are orthogonal. H₁₀ and H₀₁ are orthogonal because the first lies in U and the second in U⊥.
The remaining pairs are analogous. Thus the sum of all four spaces is an orthogonal direct sum, not merely an algebraic sum.
slides.takeaway: The four intersections are pairwise orthogonal because their membership conditions conflict.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 045000 · Why those spaces are orthogonal

slides.title: A six-dimensional example
slides.lead: Let U=span(e₁,e₂,e₅) and V=span(e₁,e₃,cosθ e₅+sinθ e₆).
body: Here 0<θ<π/2. The common space H₁₁ is span(e₁), the U-only space H₁₀ is span(e₂), the V-only space H₀₁ is span(e₃), and H₀₀ is span(e₄).
The two remaining directions e₅,e₆ form one generic tilted plane. We can now read the whole pair of projections directly from elementary one-dimensional blocks plus one two-dimensional C–S block.
slides.takeaway: The decomposition makes the whole six-dimensional projection pair explicit.

slides.title: The generic remainder is reducing
slides.lead: Take G to be the orthogonal complement of the elementary sum.
body: Each H_ab is invariant under P and Q because each projection acts there as either I or 0. Their sum therefore is invariant under both projections.
Since P and Q are self-adjoint, the orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is invariant too. Hence G is reducing for both operators.
slides.takeaway: The generic part can be studied independently of every endpoint intersection.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 045000 · The generic remainder is reducing

slides.title: Why the generic part contains no endpoint directions
slides.lead: All four elementary intersections disappear when restricted to G.
body: Suppose x in G also belongs to U∩V. Then x belongs to H₁₁, but G is perpendicular to H₁₁; consequently x=0. The same argument applies to the other three intersections.
The generic part therefore has no common direction and no nonzero source-only, target-only, or neither-only direction.
slides.takeaway: Generic position means the four membership intersections are all trivial.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 045000 · Why the generic part contains no endpoint directions

slides.title: The generic C–S block
slides.lead: In finite dimensions, G decomposes into principal planes with angles strictly between 0 and π/2.
body: On each plane, P is diag(1,0) and Q has the [[c²,cs],[cs,s²]] form. All elementary 0- and 90-degree directions were removed before these blocks were introduced.
Thus the Halmos picture consists of four easy endpoint spaces and a collection of genuinely tilted cosine–sine blocks.
slides.takeaway: On the generic part, the only remaining geometry is the principal-angle geometry.

slides.title: Infinite-dimensional caution: no uniform gap from injectivity
slides.lead: An operator can have no zero eigenvector and still fail to be bounded below.
body: For example, consider independent generic principal planes whose angles θ_n approach π/2 without ever reaching it. Every cosθ_n is positive, so no paired cosine direction vanishes.
Yet inf cosθ_n=0. The cosine operator is injective but has no bounded inverse on its range. This is why infinite-dimensional angle results need careful spectral and closed-range hypotheses.
slides.takeaway: No right-angle eigenvector does not imply a uniform acute-angle bound.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 045000 · Infinite-dimensional caution: no uniform gap from injectivity

slides.title: Defect dimensions are invariants
slides.lead: A unitary change of ambient coordinates preserves the dimensions of all four elementary spaces.
body: If one projection pair has a nonzero U-only defect and another does not, no simultaneous unitary equivalence of the pairs can erase that difference.
The generic angles also matter: two pairs with the same elementary dimensions but different principal-angle data need not be unitarily equivalent.
slides.takeaway: Endpoint multiplicities and generic angle data are part of the geometry of a projection pair.

slides.title: Reconstruct the six-dimensional pair
slides.lead: Identify all four elementary subspaces, then derive the final generic block.
body: For U=span(e₁,e₂,e₅) and V=span(e₁,e₃,c e₅+s e₆), compute the values of P and Q on e₁ through e₄. Show that span(e₅,e₆) is reducing and calculate the Q block there.
Finally explain why an infinite-dimensional generic pair may have strictly positive individual cosines without a uniform lower bound.
slides.takeaway: Halmos’s decomposition is a complete bookkeeping system for two orthogonal projections.
